I'm 53 years old and I've been farming these 22.5 mu for 33 years. Never went to school, but I know my land better than any book. There are three of us at home, and my son works in the factory in town, so most days it's just me and my wife handling the fields. I can't be everywhere, so I have to think hard about where my labor and money go.

The wheat-maize double crop is my backbone—that's 15.5 mu of my best flat land. The wheat went in last October and is greening up now. I buy improved wheat seed from the supply shop every few years—not the most expensive kind, but reliable. For fertilizer, I do what I did last year: I spread compound fertilizer before the first irrigation, then topdress urea when the wheat starts jointing. My neighbor Wang puts on more, but I watch my cash. The well gives me water, but pumping costs electricity, so I irrigate three times for wheat—green-up, jointing, and grain filling. I spray when I see aphids or weeds, usually four times total, including one fungicide if the weather turns damp. I expect about 450 kg per mu if it doesn't get too dry.

Maize goes in that same field right after wheat harvest in mid-June. There's no time to plough—I've planted directly into the wheat stubble for years now, like everyone in the village. I use hybrid seed, always. I put down fertilizer at planting and side-dress when the plants are about knee-high. Two irrigations—one at planting if it's dry, one at tasseling. Three sprays for insects and weeds. I usually get around 500 kg per mu.

The rest of the land I spread around so one bad crop doesn't ruin me. Cotton on 3.5 mu—it's heavy work, needs spraying almost every week for bollworm, maybe 14 times total, but the price has been decent. Peanut on 1.5 mu, millet on 1 mu for our own porridge, mung bean on 1 mu. These smaller plots I mostly plant with seed I saved from last year. I run the rotary tiller through them because the ground is soft. They get some compound fertilizer, but less than the wheat. Millet and mung bean hardly need watering—once is enough if the rains come. Peanut gets two irrigations.

It's a balancing act. Every yuan I spend on cotton pesticide is a yuan I don't have for wheat fertilizer. But I've farmed long enough to know that if you skip on the wheat, you lose the whole year. So wheat and maize get the first share of my money and my time.
